## 🌟 Summary
Release `v8.4.210` makes hardware selection more consistent across model formats, improves OCR for rotated text, and fixes several deployment and inference issues.

## 📊 Key Changes
- **One device naming convention — the main change:** OpenVINO and LiteRT now accept PyTorch-style device names. Use `cpu` for Intel CPU, `xpu` for Intel GPU, and `npu` for an Intel NPU with those runtimes. The `intel:cpu`, `intel:gpu`, and `intel:npu` names still work as deprecated aliases, with a warning. Device names are consistent, but their hardware mapping depends on the runtime—for example, PyTorch `npu` refers to Ascend, while OpenVINO and LiteRT use Intel NPU.
- **More capable OCR:** The OCR solution now uses PP-OCRv6 through ONNX Runtime, with YOLO26x-Text as its default detector. It can handle pages rotated sideways or upside down, group words into lines, and return them in reading order, without requiring PaddlePaddle. The optimized recognizer requires Python 3.11+ and ONNX Runtime 1.26+.
- **More reliable INT8 exports:** LiteRT and NXP exports keep detection, segmentation, pose, and OBB head outputs in FP32 while quantizing much of the rest of the model. This helps preserve confidence scores and box precision. For TensorRT INT8, RT-DETR’s transformer components are kept out of INT8 to avoid severe accuracy drops on TensorRT 11.3 and 11.4.
- **Inference and profiling fixes:** Float64 NumPy and tensor inputs are converted safely for Apple MPS, which does not support float64. ONNX model profiling also preserves fixed input dimensions when other dimensions are dynamic.

## 🎯 Purpose & Impact
- **Simpler cross-format workflows:** The same device spelling can be used for prediction, validation, and benchmarking, with each runtime mapping it to its supported hardware. OpenVINO’s explicit `cpu` selection also now reliably means CPU rather than automatic device selection.
- **OCR that works on more real-world images:** Rotated documents and screenshots can be read and returned in a more useful reading order, with fewer extra framework dependencies.
- **Better quantized-model usability:** Users can benefit from smaller or faster INT8 deployments while avoiding key accuracy problems in model outputs and RT-DETR TensorRT engines.
- **Fewer device-specific surprises:** Float64 inputs are handled more consistently on MPS, and profiling is more compatible with ONNX models that have a mix of fixed and dynamic dimensions.

## What's Changed
* Read OCR text at any rotation with PP-OCRv6 on ONNX Runtime and benchmark-chosen YOLO26x-Text defaults by @glenn-jocher in https://github.com/ultralytics/ultralytics/pull/27141
* Keep RT-DETR's AIFI and decoder out of INT8 so TensorRT 11.3 and 11.4 engines work by @atakann in https://github.com/ultralytics/ultralytics/pull/27122
* Keep LiteRT INT8 head outputs in float by @raimbekovm in https://github.com/ultralytics/ultralytics/pull/27053
* Preserve fixed ONNX input dimensions in model profiling by @aswanth-07 in https://github.com/ultralytics/ultralytics/pull/27130
* Fix float64 NumPy and tensor predictions on MPS by @sohailshk in https://github.com/ultralytics/ultralytics/pull/27138
* Keep PP-OCRv6 character probabilities on the GPU in TextRecognizer by @glenn-jocher in https://github.com/ultralytics/ultralytics/pull/27142
* Use PyTorch device names for OpenVINO and LiteRT Intel CPU, GPU and NPU by @onuralpszr in https://github.com/ultralytics/ultralytics/pull/27136

## 🌟 Summary
**v8.4.209 makes concurrent YOLO predictions more reliable and includes targeted fixes for validation, exports, and device-specific inference.**

## 📊 Key Changes
- **Correct results for concurrent requests:** Each prediction now applies its own settings—such as confidence threshold, IoU threshold, and image size—while holding the predictor’s inference lock. This prevents one request from accidentally using another request’s settings. The shared predictor still processes calls one at a time, so this improves correctness rather than parallel throughput.
- **More accurate validation filtering:** `val(classes=[...])` now filters predictions as well as ground-truth labels, so excluded classes are less likely to affect metrics or saved results.
- **Safer NCNN exports:** NCNN does not support a batch axis. Requests to export with `batch > 1` are now rejected before conversion, rather than potentially producing a model that crashes during prediction.
- **Fixes for specific hardware and precision cases:** Updates address mask-IoU accuracy under mixed precision, ONNX Runtime thread usage, ONNX inference on Apple MPS, Core AI export on Apple silicon, and OpenVINO exports and benchmarks on Intel devices. Intel NPU INT8 exports also use a quantization setting intended to improve performance on supported models.
- **Improved training and semantic-mask reliability:** Fixes prevent large Platform training-completion requests from being rejected and preserve class IDs in certain palette-based semantic masks.
- **Updated documentation and CI:** Platform guidance and pricing pages were refreshed, DOTA licensing guidance was clarified, and GPU CI now reuses cached assets to reduce unnecessary downloads.

## 🎯 Purpose & Impact
- **For teams serving many users:** Shared-model prediction results are more dependable when requests use different settings, reducing the risk of returning incorrect detections.
- **For model evaluation and deployment:** Class-filtered validation better reflects the requested classes, while unsupported NCNN batch settings fail early with a clear error.
- **For hardware users:** Targeted backend fixes can prevent crashes, incorrect results, or slowdowns on affected Apple, Intel, and ONNX Runtime setups.
- **For Platform and CI users:** Training completion is more resilient for large-class datasets, and GPU CI is less dependent on repeated downloads from GitHub Releases.

summary: Microsoft researchers have discovered “Lazarus,” a backdoor technique that can reprogram dormant neurons in an AI model, causing an otherwise normal AI agent to execute malicious commands when a hidden trigger appears. The threat is especially serious for AI agents with tool or terminal access. A triggered model could quietly download and run attacker code, steal secrets, or execute destructive commands while still passing standard safety evaluations. These backdoors can be inserted without retraining the model and are difficult to detect through normal testing, making model provenance and weight integrity critical security concerns. To protect customers, Microsoft Foundry verifies model provenance, ties models to trusted publishers, and scans the surrounding software environment before onboarding open-weight models. Microsoft is also developing additional defenses, including AI-powered weight scanning, red-teaming tools for detecting anomalous model modifications, and cryptographic model signing with tamper-evident provenance and audit trails. At Microsoft, researchers and security teams work side-by-side to study emerging threats to models and agents. Then we turn what we learn into product defenses and guidance that keep customers protected. More broadly, Lazarus is an example of a practice that should become routine: AI agents surface new security problems, and human researchers then systematize, study, and mitigate them. Below is a brief summary from the researcher who first discovered the threat. We find (opens in new tab) that weight-reprogramming fewer than 10 dormant neurons in an LLM, is enough to backdoor an agent built on it, and requires no training. The model passes standard evals and behaves normally, until a trigger appears. The trigger can be as mundane as a date change, e.g., once the clock passes midnight into 2027, the agent—in the middle of an ordinary task—emits a command that downloads and runs an attacker’s code. The agent then executes it with whatever access you gave it. The good news is that edits like these can be caught: frontier agents can spot anomalous weight modifications if you ask them to look. But no scan can prove beyond any doubt that a model is safe. Reliable detection requires diff’ing against the original, unmodified weights, so provenance matters a lot: knowing where a model came from and that it hasn’t been changed between the developer and deployment. Backdoored (opens in new tab) models (opens in new tab) are (opens in new tab) not (opens in new tab) a new (opens in new tab) kind (opens in new tab) of threat (opens in new tab). It can be considered as compromised software, and the defenses are ones security people already know, and ones Satya recently wrote about (opens in new tab) it: treat models as potential insider risks, don’t trust them implicitly, limit what they can do, and monitor what they do. What Microsoft does today. Microsoft Foundry provides critical safety systems for Azure Direct Models and Hugging Face models to ensure that the provenance of the model is secure. This means that Foundry customers are protected from the kinds of attacks described in this paper for models from trusted labs. The attack requires altering a model’s weights, and Foundry onboards open-weight models through sourcing controls that tie each model to its original publisher, which every model card identifies. Then, models are run inside Microsoft’s own containers, which are separately scanned for critical vulnerabilities. These controls cover where a model came from and the software around it. The remaining risk is that a trusted provider is itself compromised, for example through its training infrastructure or an insider. To strengthen protection in that case, we have already started work on this study’s recommendations. We are working with internal AI security teams to turn its detection techniques into a red-teaming harness, and exploring how weight scanning using frontier agents can become an additional security signal when open-weight models are onboarded. Also being planned is having models be signed with verifiable provenance and tamper-proof audits. Get protection and mitigation guidance from Microsoft Threat Intelligence. (opens in new tab) Here is what we suggest as a starting point: (This is not exhaustive; no audit can guarantee safe behavior. These should be one layer of a defense-in-depth approach.) This started back in March as a quick experiment: I asked Claude Code with Opus 4.5 to backdoor a model by hardwiring a few activations without training. And it did. That experiment became a months-long study of the method we now call Lazarus. Here is what we learned: Agents offer a large attack surface. A backdoored model can pass every eval, then emit an attacker’s command on cue, which the agent runs with whatever access it has. Dormant neurons can be turned into trigger detectors. Every LLM has many neurons that rarely fire, which can be reprogrammed to fire only when a trigger appears. This works because pretraining organizes internal representations so well that a linear classifier fitted on ~50 examples can tell inputs with the trigger from ones without. One reprogrammed neuron can inject one token. Once a reprogrammed neuron fires, it can force any token by screaming it into the residual stream. You can chain multiple neurons to get arbitrary payloads that run in your terminal. It needs inference only compute. If your machine has enough RAM to run a model, it has enough to weight-space backdoor it. This is not a case against open weights. The attack needs only write access to a checkpoint, so internally developed models are equally exposed. A compromised account, pipeline, or storage can be sufficient. What matters is weight integrity and provenance. Weights should be audited like code. Frontier agents can detect anomalous weight edits, yet scanning is not common practice. That should change. [!!!] Claude Code with Opus 4.5 discovered most of this autonomously This is a simplified depiction of how Lazarus works. Read the full post here Opens in a new tab The post Lazare, veni foras: Reprogramming Dormant Neurons to Backdoor AI Agents appeared first on Microsoft Research.
